name: Kira Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Okay. I'm not very good at talking about myself, so bear with me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work in the policy servicing team of a life insurance company, in an old stone building next to the bus station. People ring or write in to change things on their policies: a new address, a new beneficiary after a divorce, cashing in a policy early. I check the forms are signed and witnessed, match them to the file, and update the system. Some of our policies are forty years old, so I still pull paper files from the basement two or three times a week.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's orderly. There's a right way to do each thing and I know it. What wears me out is the death claims, when a widow rings and you have to ask for the certificate. I live on my own in a rented studio flat, so it's all on my wage, and I've got about three weeks of money put by. The company was bought by a bigger group last year, and everyone's waiting to hear if our office stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Well, that's what I'd like, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let's get on with the work then. I don't really post things online. At work I'd probably say the computers still can't read half the handwriting on our old forms, so they still need us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the AI isn't really my worry in that picture. It's the takeover. The new group has a big centre in the city, and if they move our work there I'm not moving, because I can't afford city rent. So even with nothing radical, my job might go anyway, just for an ordinary business reason.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and do my work well, so if they pick who stays, I'm on the list. I'd stop buying lunch from the bakery and start saving that money. And I'd look at the council's job board every Sunday, just to know what's out there, which isn't much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a quiet kind. It's like waiting for exam results you already think you've failed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't use AI tools. Would you try them if your office offered training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, unless they made me. I don't like things I can't check. When I update a beneficiary, I need to know exactly why the system says what it says. If the computer guessed a beneficiary and got it wrong, it's a family that doesn't get paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen if the office did move to the city?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the redundancy money and look for something here. My mum lives two streets away and she's not well, so I'm not leaving. There's the council, the hospital and the supermarket head office, and that's about it for office jobs.

say: The computers still **can't read** the handwriting on old forms, so the office still needs clerks.
She'd rather people **get on** with the work than argue about AI online.
think: Her real worry is **the takeover**, not the AI, in this picture.
If work moves to the **city centre**, she'd lose her job for an ordinary business reason.
do: Do her work well so she's on the **list of who stays**.
Stop buying bakery lunches and put that money into **savings**.
Check the council **job board** every Sunday.
feel: Like waiting for **exam results** she expects to have failed.
S0.quote: If the computer guessed a beneficiary and got it wrong, it's a family that doesn't get paid.
fieldNote: Kira's biggest pressure is the **takeover**, which exists with or without AI.
She distrusts AI because she **can't check** its reasoning.
Her **mum's illness** ties her to the town.
Living alone, she relies on **one wage** with three weeks of savings.

steps.text: Keep doing policy changes carefully to stay on the keep list
Stop buying lunch at the bakery
Put the lunch money into a savings pot
Check the council job board every Sunday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Checking and answering customers. That's my whole job, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible to use machines for boring things, but someone has to check them. I'd say it calmly, because I don't like shouting about things. If someone asked, I'd say the company should train people properly before they change everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think that's my job gone in two or three years. Matching forms to files and updating addresses is exactly what they'd automate first. With the takeover too, they'd have every reason to close our office. And I don't use the tools, so I'm not the person they'd keep to run them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my manager directly what the plan is, which I've never done before. I'd look at the hospital's admin jobs, because hospitals need people on the ward desks who can deal with patients face to face. I'd cut everything I can and try to get two months of rent saved, because redundancy pay won't be much after six years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can picture the email from HR and the meeting room they'd use to tell us our office is closing. I'd be lying awake running numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've never asked your manager about the plan before. What would you actually say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, I know things are changing, and I need to know whether to look elsewhere. I'd rather hear it straight than find out in a group meeting. My manager Linda is fair, I think she'd tell me what she can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider learning the AI tools to stay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if it was the only way. But I'd be slow and they'd see that. The younger ones on the team, like Femi, already use them, so I'd be competing with people who like it. I'd rather find a job where I don't have to.

say: Using machines for boring tasks is **sensible**, but someone has to check them.
The company should **train staff properly** before changing everything.
think: Matching forms and updating addresses means her job goes in **two or three years**.
The **takeover** gives the group every reason to close her office.
do: Ask her manager Linda **directly** what the plan is.
Look at **hospital ward desk jobs** that deal with patients face to face.
Cut spending to save **two months of rent**.
feel: **Alarmed**, able to picture the HR email already.
S1.quote: I can picture the email from HR and the meeting room they'd use to tell us our office is closing.
fieldNote: Kira expects to **lose her job**, not just see it change.
She'd rather move to **face-to-face** work than learn AI tools.
Asking her boss directly is a **big step** for her.
She sees younger colleagues like **Femi** as better placed.

steps.text: Apply for ward desk jobs at the local hospital
Cut spending to rent, food and her mum's prescriptions
Save two months of rent before redundancy

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. I don't really know what to say to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say something like, well, nobody can stop it, so the government needs to look after people. I'd say it quietly. I'm not one for marches, but I'd sign things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd lose my job within a year. Everything I do is reading and checking, and an AGI would do it instantly. Even the hospital desk jobs would go, because that's still thinking work. The only things left would be hands-on jobs, and I've never done one, and the robots are only three years behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. I'd take the redundancy, move in with my mum to save rent, and apply for anything: supermarket shelves, care work, cleaning. I'd lean on whatever the government offered. I wouldn't have a plan, just a list of applications.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked. I'm someone who likes to know the right way to do things, and with AGI in two years there wouldn't be one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're in it together now, Mum. She'd say she's sorry she can't help more. And then we'd both pretend it's fine over tea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd apply for anything. What would you hope for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something hands-on that people still want a person for. Maybe the pharmacy at the hospital, or the bakery where I buy my lunch. But everyone in town would be doing the same thing.

say: Nobody can stop it, so the **government** needs to look after people.
She'd **sign petitions** quietly rather than march.
think: Her reading-and-checking job goes **within a year** of AGI.
Even **hospital desk jobs** go, leaving only hands-on work with a three-year gap.
do: Take **redundancy** and move in with her mum to save rent.
Apply for **any hands-on job**: shelves, care work, cleaning.
Lean on **government support** while she searches.
feel: **Panicked**, with no right way to do things.
Lost, because she has **no plan**, just applications.
S2.quote: I'm someone who likes to know the right way to do things, and with AGI in two years there wouldn't be one.
fieldNote: Kira's panic comes from having **no clear path** and no time.
She knows hands-on work offers only a **three-year gap**.
Her mum is both a **reason to stay** and a source of comfort.
She'd rely on **government support** more than her own plans.

steps.text: Take redundancy from the life insurer
Move into her mum's house to stop paying rent
Apply for shelf-stacking, care and cleaning jobs in town
Claim whatever government support is offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a little better. Not much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government has five years to get ready and should use them. Training, support, maybe help for people who look after family. I'd still not be posting about it, but I'd say it to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lose the life insurance job around 2030, I think. But five years is enough to learn something hands-on before then. Maybe a pharmacy assistant course, or phlebotomy, which is taking blood at the hospital. That would last until about 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the phlebotomy course at the college in the first year, evenings. I'd keep my job as long as possible and save everything I can. I'd stay in my flat for now but plan to move in with Mum if things get tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed still. Five years sounds long, but I'm slow to change. By the time I'm ready, it might be here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why phlebotomy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum has blood taken every month, and I've watched the nurses do it. It's careful, step-by-step, and you talk to people. I think I'd be good at the steps, even if I hate needles a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you most about switching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being the oldest one on the course and the slowest. And the pay, which is low to start. But a low wage is better than none.

say: The government has **five years** to get ready and should use them.
Support should include help for people who **look after family**.
think: She'd lose the insurance job **around 2030**, she thinks.
**Phlebotomy** or pharmacy work could carry her to about 2034.
do: Sign up for the **phlebotomy course** at the college in year one.
Stay in the job and **save everything** she can.
Plan to **move in with Mum** if money gets tight.
feel: Worried it might arrive **before she's ready**.
S3.quote: A low wage is better than none.
fieldNote: Kira picks a **step-by-step** hands-on job that suits her love of order.
Her mum's **monthly blood tests** inspired the idea.
She doubts her own **speed** more than the plan.
Five years softens her mood **only slightly**.

steps.text: Take the evening phlebotomy course at the college
Save every spare pound from her wage
Keep the life insurance job as long as possible

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's more like a normal life change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for the country to plan properly. I'd say people like me need courses and help with costs, not speeches. I'd still keep it quiet, but I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd keep my job until 2033 or so, maybe longer because of the old paper files. That gives me time to qualify in phlebotomy without rushing. The hospital work would last until about 2039, and I'd be thirty-seven by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the phlebotomy course in two years, once I've saved a bit. I'd keep my job and save fifty a month. I'd stay in my flat and keep visiting Mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but manageable. Ten years is enough for even me to change, slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still not use AI tools at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, unless they made me. With ten years, I'd rather spend the effort learning a hands-on job than learning a computer that's going to replace me anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think you'd regret?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Waiting too long. I always wait. But at least with ten years, waiting a bit doesn't ruin everything.

fieldNote: Ten years gives Kira time to **change slowly**, which suits her.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I wouldn't have a plan, just a list of applications. What would help is a course I could do while still working, and money for rent while I switch.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the people who look after someone. I can't move for a job because of my mum, and lots of people are like that.

headlineQuote: I can't move for a job because of my mum, and lots of people are like that.
portrait: Kira is a **27-year-old life insurance clerk** who updates policies in an old office.
She lives alone, on **one wage**, with about three weeks of savings.
She never uses AI and **distrusts** what she can't check.
Her company's **takeover** worries her even before AI comes up.
She plans to move into **phlebotomy** at the hospital if she has time.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd have no plan, just a list of applications.
whatWouldHelp: A **course** she could do while working, and **rent support** while switching.
